As of the fall semester in 2021, Texas A&M was the largest American university with an enrollment of 72,982 students[7][82] who were pursuing degrees in 17 academic colleges. The student body originates from all 50 U.S. states and over 120 other countries. Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. The College of Liberal Arts and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences followed, enrolling 12% and 11% of the student body, respectively. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
The School of Education and Human Development and Mays Business School each enrolled 9%. The remaining schools enrolled less than 6% each. In addition, slightly more than 3% of the student body had not declared a major.[87]


As of 2019, the university enrolled the seventh-highest total of National Merit scholars in the United States and the third-highest among all public universities.[88][89] As of 2021, about 72% of the student body receives about $810 million in financial aid annually.[90] The admission rate of students who applied as undergraduates in 2020 was 63%.[91] The school is rated as "more selective" by *U.S. News & World Report*.[92][93]

<document>
<title>Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System</title>
<fragment>
* Fall enrollment — Fall enrollment is the traditional measure of student access to higher education. Fall enrollment data can be looked at by race/ethnicity; gender; enrollment status (part-time or full-time); and or level of study (undergraduate or graduate).
* Residence of first-time students — Data on the number of first-time freshmen by state of residence, along with data on the number who graduated from high school the previous year, serve to monitor the flow of students across state lines and calculate college-going rates by state. These data are collected in even-numbered years.

</fragment>
<fragment>
* Age data — The age distribution of enrolled students offers insight into the relationship between the changing demographics of college-going cohorts and enrollment in different types of postsecondary institutions. They also permit detailed projections of enrollment by institutional type and by age. * Unduplicated 12-month head count — Enrollment figures based on the unduplicated head count of students enrolled over a 12-month period is particularly valuable for institutions that use non-traditional calendar systems and offer short-term programs. [edit]

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>

* Outcome Measures - Starting with the 2015-16 collection, IPEDS collects information on the number of awards conferred and the enrollment status of four degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate student cohorts: 1) Full-time, first-time, 2) Part-time, first-time, 3) Full-time, non-first-time, and 4) Part-time, non-first-time. The reported data are for two points in time: 6-years and 8-years after a cohort enters an institution.

IPEDS collects institutional data on human resources and finances.

<document>
<title>Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System</title>
<fragment>
* Fall enrollment — Fall enrollment is the traditional measure of student access to higher education. Fall enrollment data can be looked at by race/ethnicity; gender; enrollment status (part-time or full-time); and or level of study (undergraduate or graduate).
* Residence of first-time students — Data on the number of first-time freshmen by state of residence, along with data on the number who graduated from high school the previous year, serve to monitor the flow of students across state lines and calculate college-going rates by state. These data are collected in even-numbered years.

</fragment>
<fragment>
* Age data — The age distribution of enrolled students offers insight into the relationship between the changing demographics of college-going cohorts and enrollment in different types of postsecondary institutions. They also permit detailed projections of enrollment by institutional type and by age. Because a student's dependency status is strongly related to age, the data can be used to provide estimates of the number of independent and dependent students attending postsecondary institutions. These data are collected in odd-numbered years.
* Unduplicated 12-month head count — Enrollment figures based on the unduplicated head count of students enrolled over a 12-month period is particularly valuable for institutions that use non-traditional calendar systems and offer short-term programs. Because this enrollment measure encompasses an entire year, it provides a more complete picture of the number of students these schools serve.

</fragment>
<fragment>
IPEDS collects institutional pricing data from institutions for full-time, first-time degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate students. This includes tuition and fee data as well as information on the estimated student budgets for students based on living situations (on-campus or off-campus).



### Admissions

[edit]

Basic information is collected from institutions that do not have an open-admissions policy on the undergraduate selection process for first-time, degree/certificate-seeking students. This includes information about admissions considerations, admissions yields, and SAT and ACT test scores.



### Enrollment

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>
<fragment>
* First–Year Retention Rates — The first-year retention rate measures the percentage of first-year students who had persisted in or completed their educational program a year later. These data have been collected since 2003.
* Graduation Rates — Graduation rate data provide information on institutional productivity and help institutions comply with reporting requirements of the Student Right-to-Know Act.
* Outcome Measures - Starting with the 2015-16 collection, IPEDS collects information on the number of awards conferred and the enrollment status of four degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate student cohorts: 1) Full-time, first-time, 2) Part-time, first-time, 3) Full-time, non-first-time, and 4) Part-time, non-first-time. The reported data are for two points in time: 6-years and 8-years after a cohort enters an institution.


### Institutional resources

[edit]

IPEDS collects institutional data on human resources and finances.




</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Ohio State University</title>
<fragment>

For the Class of 2025 (enrolled fall 2021), Ohio State received 58,180 applications and accepted 33,269 (57.2%). Of those accepted, 8,423 enrolled, a yield rate (the percentage of accepted students who choose to attend the university) of 25.3%. OSU's freshman retention rate is 93.9%, with 88% going on to graduate within six years.[68]


Of the 21% of the incoming freshman class who submitted SAT scores; the middle 50 percent Composite scores were 1260–1420.[68] Of the 64% of enrolled freshmen in 2021 who submitted ACT scores; the middle 50 percent Composite score was between 26 and 32.[68][71][72] In the 2020–2021 academic year, 26 freshman students were National Merit Scholars.[73][74]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Tuition and fees for full-time, Ohio residents enrolled at the Columbus campus for the 2014–2015 academic year were $10,037.[75] For the 2006–2007 academic year, tuition at Ohio State for Ohio residents placed it as the fifth-most expensive public university and slightly beneath the weighted average tuition of $8,553 among Ohio's thirteen public four-year universities.[76]






</fragment>
<fragment>
Public university in Columbus, Ohio, U.S.

This article is about the Columbus campus. For other campuses, see Ohio State University (disambiguation). Not to be confused with Ohio University.

![](image)An open domed room anchors the Ohio University atop the hillside where the Hocking River had cut.
At the beginning of the 20th century, less than 1,000 colleges with 160,000 students existed in the US. The number of colleges skyrocketed in waves, during the early and mid-20th century. State universities grew from small institutions of fewer than 1,000 students to campuses with 40,000 more students, with networks of regional campuses around the state. In turn, regional campuses broke away and became separate universities. [*citation needed*]


To handle the explosive growth of K–12 education, every state set up a network of teachers' colleges, beginning with Massachusetts in the 1830s. After 1950, they became state colleges and then state universities with a broad curriculum.[*citation needed*]


Major new trends included the development of the junior colleges. They were usually set up by city school systems starting in the 1920s.[35] By the 1960s they were renamed as "community colleges".

In 2019, the National Center for Education Statistics continued to project that higher education enrollment would remain stagnant, but white enrollment would drop 8 percent from 2016 to 2027. The report projected black enrollment to increase by 6 percent, Hispanic enrollment to increase 14 percent, Asian/Pacific Islander enrollment to increase 7 percent, and American Indian/Alaska Native enrollment to decrease 9 percent during the same period.[13] In March 2019, Moody's warned that enrollment declines could lead to more financial problems for the higher education industry.[205] In a 2019 survey by *Inside Higher Ed*, nearly one in seven college presidents said their campus could close or merge within five years.[206] The total number of degree granting colleges in the US peaked in 2012 and has decreased every year since then.[207]

Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. <title>Texas A&M University</title>
<fragment>
As of the fall semester in 2021, Texas A&M was the largest American university with an enrollment of 72,982 students[7][82] who were pursuing degrees in 17 academic colleges. The student body originates from all 50 U.S. states and over 120 other countries. Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. The College of Liberal Arts and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences followed, enrolling 12% and 11% of the student body, respectively.

Based on my search results, I was able to find the total enrollment figure for Texas A&M University in Fall 2023, but unfortunately, I could not locate the specific undergraduate enrollment breakdown from the available Wikipedia sources.

Here's what I found:

## Available Information from Wikipedia Sources:

**Total Fall 2023 Enrollment:** 77,491 students
- Source: "List of public universities in Texas by enrollment"
- Data from Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board (THECB)

## Limitations:

Unfortunately, the Wikipedia articles I searched did not contain the specific undergraduate vs. graduate enrollment breakdown for Fall 2023. The available sources showed:

1. **2021 data**: Texas A&M had 72,982 students (but didn't specify undergraduate vs. graduate split)
2. **Fall 2023 total**: 77,491 students (confirmed total enrollment figure you mentioned)

## Recommendations:

To find the specific undergraduate enrollment figure for Fall 2023, I would recommend checking:

1. **Texas A&M University's official website** - Look for their Office of Institutional Research or enrollment statistics pages
2. **Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board (THECB)** - They provided the total enrollment figures and may have more detailed breakdowns
3. **Texas A&M's Common Data Set for 2023-2024** - This typically contains detailed enrollment breakdowns by undergraduate/graduate status
4. **IPEDS (Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System)** - Federal database with detailed enrollment statistics

The 77,491 total enrollment figure you found appears to be accurate for Fall 2023, but the specific undergraduate component would need to be obtained from more detailed institutional sources that go beyond what's available in Wikipedia articles.

	+ This 324-acre (131 ha) research park was established to provide businesses direct partnering opportunities with Texas A&M University. 	+ Crescent Pointe is a master-planned, mixed-use development of roughly 192 acres (78 ha), with frontage on University Drive (FM 60) and Harvey Road (Highway 30).

Based on my research of Wikipedia sources, I can provide you with official enrollment information for Texas A&M University in the 2023 academic year:

## Texas A&M University Enrollment 2023

According to the Wikipedia article "List of public universities in Texas by enrollment," which cites data from the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board, **Texas A&M University had a record enrollment of 77,491 students in Fall 2023**.

### Additional Context:
- This represents a significant increase from the previous year (2022: 74,829 students)
- The 2023 enrollment made Texas A&M the largest university in Texas
- This appears to be a record enrollment level for the university

### Historical Comparison from Wikipedia Data:
| Year | Enrollment |
|------|------------|
| 2023 | **77,491** |
| 2022 | 74,829 |
| 2021 | 66,057 |
| 2020 | 65,272 |
| 2015 | 58,515 |
| 2012 | 56,378 |

The data shows a remarkable growth trend, particularly the jump from 2022 to 2023, which represents an increase of approximately 2,662 students in just one year.

**Note:** This information is based on the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board data as referenced in the Wikipedia article. For the most detailed breakdown of enrollment demographics and methodology, you would need to consult the official Texas A&M University Institutional Research office or the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board directly.

Based on my Wikipedia searches, here's what I found regarding Texas A&M's Fall 2023 enrollment data:

## Key Findings from Wikipedia:

### Total Enrollment Confirmed
The Wikipedia article **"List of public universities in Texas by enrollment"** confirms that **Texas A&M University had 77,491 total students in Fall 2023**, which made it the largest university in Texas.

### Source Information
The Wikipedia article cites as its source: **"THECB - Enrollment" from Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board (retrieved August 27, 2023)**

### Historical Context from Wikipedia
- **2023**: 77,491 students (record enrollment)
- **2022**: 74,829 students 
- This represents an increase of 2,662 students in one year

## What I Did NOT Find in Wikipedia:

<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities

 |




</fragment>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model

[edit]

2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, there is **no comprehensive evidence confirming that Texas A&M University has surpassed University of Central Florida (UCF) as the largest university by enrollment**. Here's what the available data shows:

## Key Findings:

### Texas A&M University's Recent Growth (2022-2023)
- **2023 enrollment**: 77,491 students (all levels)
- **2022 enrollment**: 74,829 students  
- **Significant growth**: ~3.5k students in one year
- This represents remarkable growth, making Texas A&M the largest public university **in Texas**

### Latest Available Rankings
From Wikipedia's most recent comprehensive lists:
- **2020 rankings**: UCF (71,881) ranked #9, Texas A&M (70,418) ranked #10 nationally
- **2018-19 (undergraduate-only)**: UCF (58,913) ranked #1, Texas A&M (54,369) ranked #2
- **Florida state institutions show strong growth trends** in all available periods

### Data Limitations
The search revealed several important gaps:
- **No 2023 national rankings** are available in Wikipedia articles
- **No Florida university system 2023 enrollment data** accessible
- Most recent comprehensive national data is from 2020
- Texas A&M's dramatic recent growth may not be reflected in national comparisons yet

## Conclusion:
While Texas A&M has shown **impressive enrollment growth in 2023**, reaching 77,491 students and **becoming the largest university in Texas**, there is **insufficient current data** to confirm whether it has surpassed UCF as the largest university nationally. UCF has historically held this position, but updated national enrollment comparisons for 2023 are not available in the current Wikipedia sources consulted.

The most recent complete national comparison shows UCF still leading, but Texas A&M's trajectory suggests it could potentially overtake UCF when updated national rankings become available.

<document>
<title>Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System</title>
<fragment>
IPEDS collects institutional pricing data from institutions for full-time, first-time degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate students. This includes tuition and fee data as well as information on the estimated student budgets for students based on living situations (on-campus or off-campus).



### Admissions

[edit]

Basic information is collected from institutions that do not have an open-admissions policy on the undergraduate selection process for first-time, degree/certificate-seeking students. This includes information about admissions considerations, admissions yields, and SAT and ACT test scores.



### Enrollment

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>
<fragment>
U.S. core higher education data collection program



Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System| ![](image)Logo of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System
 |
| Established | 1992 |


The **Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System** (**IPEDS**) is a system of interrelated surveys conducted annually by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), a part of the Institute for Education Sciences within the United States Department of Education. IPEDS consists of twelve interrelated survey components that are collected over three collection periods (fall, winter, and spring) each year as described in the Data Collection and Dissemination Cycle. The completion of all IPEDS surveys is mandatory for all institutions that participate in, or are applicants for participation in, any federal financial assistance program authorized by Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended.[1]


The IPEDS program department of NCES was created in 1992 and began collecting data in 1993.




</fragment>
<fragment>

## Data collected in IPEDS

[edit]

IPEDS collects data on postsecondary education in the United States in the following areas: institutional characteristics, institutional prices, admissions, enrollment, student financial aid, degrees and certificates conferred, student persistence and success (retention rates, graduation rates, and outcome measures), institutional human resources, fiscal resources, and academic libraries.[1]



### Institutional characteristics

[edit]

Institutional characteristics data are the foundation of the entire IPEDS system. These include basic institutional contact information, tuition and fees, room and board charges, control or affiliation, type of calendar system, levels of awards offered, types of programs, and admissions requirements.



### Institutional prices

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
IPEDS collects data on the number of students who complete a postsecondary education program by type of program and level of award (certificate or degree). Type of program is categorized according to the Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP), a detailed coding system for postsecondary instructional programs. These data provide information on the number and location of completers by field. Business and industry, the military, and other groups that need to recruit individuals with particular skills use these data extensively. The data also help satisfy the mandate in the Carl D. Perkins Vocational and Technical Education Act for information on completions in postsecondary career and technical education programs.



### Student persistence and success

[edit]

IPEDS collects two types of data to help track postsecondary student progress and success.




</fragment>
</document>

IPEDS collects institutional pricing data from institutions for full-time, first-time degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate students. This includes tuition and fee data as well as information on the estimated student budgets for students based on living situations (on-campus or off-campus).



### Admissions

[edit]

Basic information is collected from institutions that do not have an open-admissions policy on the undergraduate selection process for first-time, degree/certificate-seeking students. This includes information about admissions considerations, admissions yields, and SAT and ACT test scores.



### Enrollment

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>
<fragment>
U.S. core higher education data collection program



Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System| ![](image)Logo of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System
 |
| Established | 1992 |


The **Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System** (**IPEDS**) is a system of interrelated surveys conducted annually by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), a part of the Institute for Education Sciences within the United States Department of Education. IPEDS consists of twelve interrelated survey components that are collected over three collection periods (fall, winter, and spring) each year as described in the Data Collection and Dissemination Cycle. The completion of all IPEDS surveys is mandatory for all institutions that participate in, or are applicants for participation in, any federal financial assistance program authorized by Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended.[1]


The IPEDS program department of NCES was created in 1992 and began collecting data in 1993.




</fragment>
<fragment>

## Data collected in IPEDS

[edit]

IPEDS collects data on postsecondary education in the United States in the following areas: institutional characteristics, institutional prices, admissions, enrollment, student financial aid, degrees and certificates conferred, student persistence and success (retention rates, graduation rates, and outcome measures), institutional human resources, fiscal resources, and academic libraries.[1]



### Institutional characteristics

[edit]

Institutional characteristics data are the foundation of the entire IPEDS system. These include basic institutional contact information, tuition and fees, room and board charges, control or affiliation, type of calendar system, levels of awards offered, types of programs, and admissions requirements.

<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities



|  |  |  |  |  |  |

Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.*Find sources:* "Common Data Set" – news **·** newspapers **·** books **·** scholar **·** JSTOR *(July 2010)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |




</fragment>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

</fragment>

<fragment>
As of the fall semester in 2021, Texas A&M was the largest American university with an enrollment of 72,982 students[7][82] who were pursuing degrees in 17 academic colleges. The student body originates from all 50 U.S. states and over 120 other countries. Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. The College of Liberal Arts and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences followed, enrolling 12% and 11% of the student body, respectively.

<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.

## External links

[edit]

</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

<title>Texas A&M University</title>
<fragment>
As of the fall semester in 2021, Texas A&M was the largest American university with an enrollment of 72,982 students[7][82] who were pursuing degrees in 17 academic colleges. The student body originates from all 50 U.S. states and over 120 other countries. Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. The College of Liberal Arts and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences followed, enrolling 12% and 11% of the student body, respectively.

<title>Texas A&M University</title>
<fragment>
As of the fall semester in 2021, Texas A&M was the largest American university with an enrollment of 72,982 students[7][82] who were pursuing degrees in 17 academic colleges. The student body originates from all 50 U.S. states and over 120 other countries. Texas residents account for 86.27% of the student population and 7.42% are of international origin.[83] The demographics of the student body are 52.9% male and 47.1% female.[84] Members of ethnic minority groups make up 42.2% of the student population.[a] According to *U.S. News & World Report*, Texas A&M has a student-to-teacher ratio of 19:1 and an average-freshman-retention rate of 92%.[84][85] According to the institution, in 2019, it had a four-year-graduation rate of 59% and a six-year-graduation of 81.7%.[86] College of Engineering had the largest enrollment of 29.6%. The College of Liberal Arts and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences followed, enrolling 12% and 11% of the student body, respectively.

<document>
<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities



|  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ![](image)
 | **This article has multiple issues.** Please help **improve it** or discuss these issues on the **talk page**. *(Learn how and when to remove these messages)*
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![](image)
 | This article **needs additional citations for verification**. Please help improve this article by adding citations to reliable sources. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.*Find sources:* "Common Data Set" – news **·** newspapers **·** books **·** scholar **·** JSTOR *(July 2010)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |




</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]

</fragment>

<document>
<title>List of the largest United States colleges and universities by enrollment</title>
<fragment>
The United States Department of Education's Integrated Post-secondary Education Data System contains information on all 6,125 officially recognized institutions of higher education in the United States. - I couldn't find specific 2023 enrollment data on Wikipedia

- Institutional research office enrollment reports
- IPEDS detailed breakdowns

3. **State higher education agencies** (like the THECB for Texas)

The Wikipedia data suggests Texas A&M had significant growth from 2022 to 2023 (+2,662 students), which would support your argument that they're closing the gap with larger universities.

Based on my search using Wikipedia, I was unable to find specific Arizona State University Fall 2023 enrollment data. Here's what I discovered and the limitations I encountered:

## Limitations of Available Search Tools

The search function I have access to only searches Wikipedia articles, not the broader web or specific university websites. Wikipedia has a significant lag in updating enrollment statistics, especially for recent semesters like Fall 2023.

## What I Was Able to Find

From the Wikipedia articles, I found the most recent ASU enrollment data available:

### **ASU Enrollment from August 2022** (not Fall 2023):
- **Total systemwide enrollment: 140,759 students** (both in-person and online)
- **In-person campus enrollment: ~79,000 students** 
- **ASU Online enrollment: ~61,000 students**
- This represented a 4% increase over 2021 totals
- Source: KTAR News, August 22, 2022

From other Wikipedia lists, ASU was ranked as:
- **7th largest in U.S.** for Fall 2020 campus immersion enrollment: 74,795 students
- This data is from 2020, not relevant to Fall 2023

- ❌ No Fall 2023 enrollment numbers found
- ❌ No official ASU press releases for Fall 2023
- ❌ No source URLs or publication dates for 2023 data
- ❌ No 2023 breakdowns (undergrad/grad, campus/online)
- ❌ No 2023 records or milestones

3. **Timing:** Fall enrollment announcements typically come out in late August or early September each year.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities



|  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ![](image)
 | **This article has multiple issues.** Please help **improve it** or discuss these issues on the **talk page**. *(Learn how and when to remove these messages)*
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![](image)
 | This article **needs additional citations for verification**. Please help improve this article by adding citations to reliable sources. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.*Find sources:* "Common Data Set" – news **·** newspapers **·** books **·** scholar **·** JSTOR *(July 2010)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |




</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>

These individual responses can provide valuable information for students applying to a particular college or university. For example, section C7 - "Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria" – indicates the admission process for that college places on items like "Class Rank", "GPA", and "Extra-Curricular Activities". Another example is Sections C9 to C12, which give a statistical breakdown of SAT/ACT scores, class rank, and GPA for the current freshman class. This can be a good indicator, especially for the more selective colleges and universities, of the typical scores needed for admission. Sections on "Tuition and Fees" and "Financial Aid" can help potential applicants to understand the typical costs and potential aid they might receive based on the current freshman class statistics.

[edit]

The CDS annual survey includes the following major sections, identified by major sections (A–J) and subsections (0, 1, 3, ...):

</document>

<document>
<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities

Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.*Find sources:* "Common Data Set" – news **·** newspapers **·** books **·** scholar **·** JSTOR *(July 2010)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |




</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

</fragment>
</document>

## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System</title>
<fragment>
IPEDS collects institutional pricing data from institutions for full-time, first-time degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate students. This includes tuition and fee data as well as information on the estimated student budgets for students based on living situations (on-campus or off-campus).



### Admissions

[edit]

Basic information is collected from institutions that do not have an open-admissions policy on the undergraduate selection process for first-time, degree/certificate-seeking students. This includes information about admissions considerations, admissions yields, and SAT and ACT test scores.



### Enrollment

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>
<fragment>
U.S. core higher education data collection program



Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System| ![](image)Logo of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System
 |
| Established | 1992 |


The **Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System** (**IPEDS**) is a system of interrelated surveys conducted annually by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), a part of the Institute for Education Sciences within the United States Department of Education. IPEDS consists of twelve interrelated survey components that are collected over three collection periods (fall, winter, and spring) each year as described in the Data Collection and Dissemination Cycle. The completion of all IPEDS surveys is mandatory for all institutions that participate in, or are applicants for participation in, any federal financial assistance program authorized by Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended.[1]


The IPEDS program department of NCES was created in 1992 and began collecting data in 1993.




</fragment>
<fragment>

## Data collected in IPEDS

[edit]

IPEDS collects data on postsecondary education in the United States in the following areas: institutional characteristics, institutional prices, admissions, enrollment, student financial aid, degrees and certificates conferred, student persistence and success (retention rates, graduation rates, and outcome measures), institutional human resources, fiscal resources, and academic libraries.[1]



### Institutional characteristics

[edit]

Institutional characteristics data are the foundation of the entire IPEDS system. These include basic institutional contact information, tuition and fees, room and board charges, control or affiliation, type of calendar system, levels of awards offered, types of programs, and admissions requirements.



### Institutional prices

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* Fall enrollment — Fall enrollment is the traditional measure of student access to higher education. Fall enrollment data can be looked at by race/ethnicity; gender; enrollment status (part-time or full-time); and or level of study (undergraduate or graduate).
* Residence of first-time students — Data on the number of first-time freshmen by state of residence, along with data on the number who graduated from high school the previous year, serve to monitor the flow of students across state lines and calculate college-going rates by state. These data are collected in even-numbered years.

</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System</title>
<fragment>
* Fall enrollment — Fall enrollment is the traditional measure of student access to higher education. Fall enrollment data can be looked at by race/ethnicity; gender; enrollment status (part-time or full-time); and or level of study (undergraduate or graduate).
* Residence of first-time students — Data on the number of first-time freshmen by state of residence, along with data on the number who graduated from high school the previous year, serve to monitor the flow of students across state lines and calculate college-going rates by state. These data are collected in even-numbered years.

</fragment>
<fragment>
IPEDS collects institutional pricing data from institutions for full-time, first-time degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate students. This includes tuition and fee data as well as information on the estimated student budgets for students based on living situations (on-campus or off-campus).



### Admissions

[edit]

Basic information is collected from institutions that do not have an open-admissions policy on the undergraduate selection process for first-time, degree/certificate-seeking students. This includes information about admissions considerations, admissions yields, and SAT and ACT test scores.



### Enrollment

[edit]

Because enrollment patterns differ greatly among the various types of postsecondary institutions, there is a need for both different measures of enrollment and several indicators of access. In IPEDS, the following enrollment-related data are collected:




</fragment>
<fragment>
* First–Year Retention Rates — The first-year retention rate measures the percentage of first-year students who had persisted in or completed their educational program a year later. These data have been collected since 2003.
* Graduation Rates — Graduation rate data provide information on institutional productivity and help institutions comply with reporting requirements of the Student Right-to-Know Act.
* Outcome Measures - Starting with the 2015-16 collection, IPEDS collects information on the number of awards conferred and the enrollment status of four degree/certificate-seeking undergraduate student cohorts: 1) Full-time, first-time, 2) Part-time, first-time, 3) Full-time, non-first-time, and 4) Part-time, non-first-time. The reported data are for two points in time: 6-years and 8-years after a cohort enters an institution.


### Institutional resources

[edit]

IPEDS collects institutional data on human resources and finances.




</fragment>
<fragment>
U.S. core higher education data collection program



Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System| ![](image)Logo of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System
 |
| Established | 1992 |


The **Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System** (**IPEDS**) is a system of interrelated surveys conducted annually by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), a part of the Institute for Education Sciences within the United States Department of Education. IPEDS consists of twelve interrelated survey components that are collected over three collection periods (fall, winter, and spring) each year as described in the Data Collection and Dissemination Cycle. The completion of all IPEDS surveys is mandatory for all institutions that participate in, or are applicants for participation in, any federal financial assistance program authorized by Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended.[1]


The IPEDS program department of NCES was created in 1992 and began collecting data in 1993.




</fragment>
</document>

* The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), which collects aggregate institutional data on more than 7,000 postsecondary institutions that participate in Title IV federal student aid programs
* The *National Postsecondary Student Aid Study* (NPSAS), a nationally representative cross-sectional study of how students and families pay for college
* The *Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study* (BPS), a nationally representative longitudinal study that follows first-time, beginning students for six years after their entry to college and provides information about students' persistence and attainment outcomes
* The *Baccalaureate and Beyond Longitudinal Study* (B&B), a nationally representative longitudinal study that follows baccalaureate graduates for up to ten years, collecting information on their early labor market experiences and post-baccalaureate training and education

<document>
<title>University of Florida</title>
<fragment>
In fall 2019, the University of Florida had 56,567 students, 37,874 (67%) being undergraduate students, 12,110 (21%) being graduate students, 3,804 (7%) being professional students, 2,644 (5%) being unclassified, and 133 (0.2%) being correspondence students. Out of all 56,567 students, 3,797 were enrolled through UF Online. The ratio of women to men was 57:43 and 28 percent were graduate or professional students. Professional degree programs include architecture, dentistry, law, medicine, pharmacy and veterinary medicine.[169] According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, UF has "the largest Jewish student body in the US."[170] It is estimated that 18% of UF undergraduate and graduate students identify as Jewish compared to around 2% of the United States population.[171]


</fragment>
<fragment>
18. **^** Nathan Crabbe, "UF is no longer largest in state as classes start; Official says UF emphasis is on quality, not quantity Archived June 15, 2011, at the Wayback Machine," *The Gainesville Sun* (August 25, 2009). Retrieved April 18, 2012.

The 2022 annual ranking of *U.S. News & World Report* categorizes the University of Florida as "most selective."[68] For the Class of 2024 (enrolled fall 2020), Florida received 48,193 applications and accepted 15,002 (31.1%). Of those accepted, 6,333 enrolled, a yield rate (the percentage of accepted students who choose to attend the university) of 42.2%. Florida's freshman retention rate is 97%, with 89% going on to graduate within six years.[69][70]


The enrolled first-year class of 2024 had the following standardized test scores: the middle 50% range (25th percentile-75th percentile) of SAT scores was 1310–1450, while the middle 50% range of ACT scores was 29–33.[69][71][72] The University of Florida has the second most selective application process of any university or college in the state of Florida, behind only the University of Miami.[73][74][75]
[76]

The university is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools (SACS). It is the third largest Florida university by student population[18] and is the fifth largest single-campus university in the United States with 57,841 students enrolled for during the 2020–21 school year.[19] The University of Florida is home to 16 academic colleges and more than 150 research centers and institutes. It offers multiple graduate professional programs—including business administration, engineering, law, dentistry, medicine, pharmacy and veterinary medicine—on one contiguous campus and administers 123 master's degree programs and 76 doctoral degree programs in 87 schools and departments. <fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]

<document>
<title>Institutional research</title>
<content>
**Institutional research** is a broad category of work done at schools, colleges and universities to inform campus decision-making and planning in areas such as admissions, financial aid, curriculum assessment, enrollment management, staffing, student life, finance, facilities, athletics, and alumni relations.


Institutional researchers collect, analyze, report, and warehouse quantitative and qualitative data about their institution's students, faculty, staff, curriculum, course offerings, and learning outcomes. They are involved in collecting and reporting information to government bodies (for example, in the US, the United States Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System), to the public (e.g., Common Data Set, the National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities's University-College Accountability Network), and various college guide publishers (e.g., U.S. News & World Report and College Board). On occasion, institutional researchers share data with one another to compare their own practices and outcomes against those of similar institutions. Institutional research is the source of much of the information provided to regional and national accreditation bodies to document how institutions fulfill the standards for accreditation.


In addition to reporting, institutional researchers often engage in data analysis, ranging from simply testing whether differences in reported data are statistically significant to developing and using causal and predictive statistical models. Such models are often used in support of assessment and strategic enrollment management.



## Becoming an Institutional Researcher

[edit]

Due to the need to provide data to the federal government and other entities, nearly every post-secondary institution has offices that fulfill the institutional research function. At some colleges and universities this function is centralized in a single office of institutional research, while at others it is more de-centralized. There is no single academic degree that qualifies one to be an institutional researcher, but suggested strengths include a knowledge of statistics, research methods (e.g., survey research and focus groups), and computer-based reporting and data visualization tools (e.g., SPSS, SAS, R, STATA, Microsoft Access, Microsoft Excel, MicroStrategy, and SQL). Other important assets are strong written and oral communications skills, attention to detail, and knowledge about how institutions of higher education operate. Several American universities offer graduate certificate programs in institutional research,[1] including Ball State University, Florida State University, Humboldt State University,[2] North Dakota State University, Penn State University, Indiana University, University of Missouri, University of Illinois, the University of Wisconsin - Stout,[3] and the University of California San Diego Extension.[4]

<document>
<title>Institutional research</title>
<fragment>

Institutional researchers collect, analyze, report, and warehouse quantitative and qualitative data about their institution's students, faculty, staff, curriculum, course offerings, and learning outcomes. They are involved in collecting and reporting information to government bodies (for example, in the US, the United States Department of Education's Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System), to the public (e.g., Common Data Set, the National Association of Independent Colleges and Universities's University-College Accountability Network), and various college guide publishers (e.g., U.S. News & World Report and College Board). On occasion, institutional researchers share data with one another to compare their own practices and outcomes against those of similar institutions. Institutional research is the source of much of the information provided to regional and national accreditation bodies to document how institutions fulfill the standards for accreditation.


</fragment>
</document>

In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>U.S. News & World Report Best Colleges Ranking</title>
<fragment>
News* has been supplying this exact college information for many years already. And it appears that NAICU will be doing it with significantly less comparability and functionality. *U.S. News* first collects all these data (using an agreed-upon set of definitions from the Common Data Set). Then we post the data on our website in easily accessible, comparable tables. In other words, the Annapolis Group and the others in the NAICU initiative actually are following the lead of *U.S. News*".[31]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* "Expert opinion" (20%): presidents, provosts and deans of admissions rate the academic quality of peer institutions with which they are familiar on a scale of 1 (marginal) to 5 (distinguished)
* "Financial resources" (8%): the average per-student spending on instruction, research, student services and related educational expenditures
* "Student selectivity" (5%): the standardized test scores of admitted students and the proportion of admitted students in upper percentiles of their high school class
* "Faculty Research" (4%): Amount of citations to papers and research attributed to faculty while employed at the college


The publication is split into four categories: National Universities, Liberal Arts Colleges, Regional Universities, and Regional Colleges, with the latter two categories further split into North, South, Midwest, and West.[12]


</fragment>
<fragment>
11. **^** Morse, Robert; Brooks, Eric (September 17, 2023). "How U.S. News Calculated the 2024 Best Colleges Rankings". *U.S. News & World Report*. Retrieved September 17, 2023.
12. **^** Leiby, Richard (September 9, 2014). "The U.S. News college rankings guru". *The Washington Post*.
13. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Gnolek, Shari L.; Falciano, Vincenzo T.; Kuncl, Ralph W. (2014). "Modeling Change and Variation in U.S. News & World Report College Rankings: What would it really take to be in the Top 20?". *Research in Higher Education*. **55** (8): 761–779. doi:10.1007/s11162-014-9336-9. S2CID 144016491.
14. **^** "2023-2024: Best National Universities" *U.S. News & World Report*
15. **^** "2023–2024: Best National Liberal Arts Colleges" *U.S. News & World Report*
16. **^** Smith, Steve (September 19, 2013). "U.S. News Pulls Social Levers to Break Records for 'Best Colleges' Package". *min Online*. Archived from the original on January 23, 2015. Retrieved July 24, 2022.

</fragment>
<fragment>

A 2014 study published in *Research in Higher Education* removed the mystique of the *U.S. News* ranking process by producing a ranking model that faithfully recreated *U.S. News* outcomes and quantified the inherent "noise" in the rankings for all nationally ranked universities.[13] The model developed provided detailed insight into the *U.S. News* ranking process. It allowed the impact of changes to *U.S. News* sub factors to be studied when variation between universities and within sub factors was present. Numerous simulations were run using this model to understand the amount of change required for a university to improve its rank or move into the top 20. Results show that for a university ranked in the mid-30s it would take a significant amount of additional resources, directed in a very focused way, to become a top-ranked national university, and that rank changes of up to +/− 4 points should be considered "noise".[13]

## Key Findings About Common Data Set Structure:

### 1. **Common Data Set Initiative**
The Common Data Set (CDS) is a collaborative effort between major education publishers (College Board, Peterson's, and U.S. News & World Report) to standardize data collection from colleges and universities. Key points from the research:

- **Data Categories**: The CDS organizes data into specific sections:
  - A – General College Information (address, classification, calendar, degrees offered)
  - B – Enrollment and Persistence (demographics, graduation rates, retention rates)
  - C – First-Time, First-Year Admissions (test scores, GPA, admission policies)
  - D – Transfer Admissions
  - E – Academic Offerings and Policies
  - F – Student Life
  - G – Annual Expenses
  - H – Financial Aid
  - I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size
  - J – Degrees Conferred

### 2. **How Universities Publish Their CDS**
According to the Wikipedia information:
> "Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the 'survey' submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, **individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.**"

### 3. **Typical URL Patterns (Based on Institutional Knowledge)**
While I couldn't find specific working examples in Wikipedia, universities typically follow these naming conventions:

**Common URL Structure Patterns:**
- `/institutional-research/common-data-set/`
- `/facts-and-figures/common-data-set/`
- `/about/common-data-set/`
- `/ir/common-data-set/`
- `/planning/common-data-set/`

**File Naming Conventions:**
- `CDS_2023-2024.pdf`
- `Common_Data_Set_2023.pdf`
- `UCFS_CDS_2024.pdf`
- `Common-Data-Set-2023-24.pdf`

### 4. **Alternative Data Sources**
Since finding specific CDS URLs proved challenging through Wikipedia, consider these alternative approaches:

**IPEDS & College Navigator:**
- Most comprehensive federal database for institutional data
- Available through the U.S. Department of Education
- Standardized data that feeds into many ranking systems

**Direct University Research:**
- Look for "Institutional Research" or "Institutional Effectiveness" offices
- Search for "Facts & Figures" or "University Profile" sections
- Check "About Us" or "Quick Facts" pages

## Recommendations for Finding UF's Common Data Set:

1. **Search UF's institutional research office** directly
2. **Look for** `ufl.edu/institutional-research/` or similar paths
3. **Try** `ufl.edu/about/facts-and-figures/`
4. **Check** `ufl.edu/ir/common-data-set/`
5. **Search for** "University of Florida Common Data Set PDF" directly

The lack of specific URL examples in Wikipedia is actually typical - each university structures these differently, and the directories aren't usually indexed in general academic databases like Wikipedia. The most reliable approach is to navigate directly through UF's website structure looking for institutional research or institutional effectiveness departments.

<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Common data definitions for US colleges and universities

Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.*Find sources:* "Common Data Set" – news **·** newspapers **·** books **·** scholar **·** JSTOR *(July 2010)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |




</fragment>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* I – Instructional Faculty and Class Size: Faculty Demographics (Men/Women, Degrees, Full/Part-Time), Student-to-Faculty Ratio, Class Counts by Section/Sub-Section Size
* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>
* A – General College Information: Address, Classification of Undergraduate Institution, Academic Year Calendar, Degrees Offered
* B – Enrollment and Persistence: Current Institutional Enrollment – Men and Women, Enrollment by Racial/Ethnic Category, Number of Degrees Awarded, Graduation Rates, Retention Rates
* C – First-Time, First-Year (Freshman) Admissions: Freshman Student Applicants (Admitted, Enrolled, Wait-Listed), Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria, Admission Requirements (Diploma, GED, College Prep Program), HS Academic Subject Requirements, Open Enrollment, SAT & ACT Policies (Requirements, Deadlines), Existing Freshman Class Statistical Profile (SAT & ACT Scoring Breakdown, Class Rank Breakdown, HS GPA Breakdown), Average GPA, Admission Policies (Application Fees, Closing Dates, Notification Date(s)), Other Admission Policies

</fragment>
</document>

<title>Common Data Set</title>
<fragment>
Each year the Common Data Set initiative makes small changes to the "survey" submitted for every contributing college and university to complete. While the resulting database of all responses is not available for download, individual colleges and universities typically publish their individual responses on their own website.


</fragment>

* J – Degrees Conferred by Disciplinary Areas


## See also

[edit]

* Common data model


## References

[edit]

1. **^** "Common Data Set Initiative". Common Data Set Initiative. Retrieved 14 May 2015.
2. **^** Association for Institutional Research (1997). "AIR Alert #1". Archived from the original on June 13, 2010. Retrieved March 23, 2010.
3. **^** Voluntary System of Accountability Program (2010), *About the College Portrait*, retrieved March 23, 2010

## External links

[edit]

* Official website

</fragment>
<fragment>

The **Common Data Set** (**CDS**) is a product of the Common Data Set Initiative, "a collaborative effort among data providers in the higher education community and publishers as represented by the College Board, Peterson's, and *U.S. News & World Report*."[1] The stated goal is to provide accurate and timely data to students and their families while decreasing the workload of administrators. In producing their popular publications and rankings, these publishers "ask the same core questions" of institutions using the Common Data Set to define those questions and their responses.[2] These data are also used in public accountability efforts such as the Voluntary System of Accountability's College Portrait.[3]




## Annual CDS survey results

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

These individual responses can provide valuable information for students applying to a particular college or university. For example, section C7 - "Relative Importance of Common Academic and Non-Academic Admission Criteria" – indicates the admission process for that college places on items like "Class Rank", "GPA", and "Extra-Curricular Activities". Another example is Sections C9 to C12, which give a statistical breakdown of SAT/ACT scores, class rank, and GPA for the current freshman class. This can be a good indicator, especially for the more selective colleges and universities, of the typical scores needed for admission. Sections on "Tuition and Fees" and "Financial Aid" can help potential applicants to understand the typical costs and potential aid they might receive based on the current freshman class statistics.
